chapter_theme: The paalai decade of separation: the woman wasting at the sight of spring (31) and fearing the road of robbers, ghouls and hero-stones (34, 35); the friend's comfort through beasts that care for their mates on that road (32, 36, 38); the mother doubting the eloping girl who has forgotten her toys and faltered at play (33, 37); and the man holding back, telling his heart of her sobs and of tomorrow's lonely bed (39, 40).

31.reading: Each time she sees the early summer, when the murukku puts out buds like a tiger's claws dyed with blood and the cool rains have gone, a season that gives joy to lovers who are together, the woman says her heart, mixed with grief, wastes away.
31.nuance: The poem names its own contrast: the season brings joy to those who meet (எதிருநர்க்கு), so her grief is measured against the pleasure the same sight gives the united. The blood-dyed claw turns the spring flower into an image of a wound.

thinai_evidence.note: the early summer, the season of paalai

comparisons.tenor: the red curved buds of the murukku

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the woman left behind, seeing the season

iraicchi.act: the tusker carries the little water of a muddy rock pool in his trunk and pours it on the head of his heat-worn mate
iraicchi.sense: the man who passes such care on his road will be moved to the same care for the wife he left

32.reading: The friend tells the bright-jewelled woman that the man is able to go across the wasteland where a handsome tusker takes up in his trunk the little water in the mud of a rock pool and pours it over the head of his mate, worn out by the heat.
32.nuance: Line 1 is hard to construe, so whether the friend means 'he is strong enough to go' or 'will he not come back?' is open; either way the tusker's care is what she offers as her argument.

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the friend comforts the waiting woman

33.reading: The mother says the girl of chosen words sweet as milk no longer thinks of her doll, her ball, her green parrot with its coral beak or her playmates; will she go after her lover through the forest that the sun's rays scorch?
33.nuance: The things she forgets are all of childhood, so their being forgotten is the sign that she has left it; the milk of her speech keeps her a child in her mother's words even as she goes.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl going with her lover into the forest

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the mother laments the eloping daughter, to no named hearer

34.reading: The friend asks the man whether he will go, leaving the woman of wide sword-bright eyes, across many wastelands where hard-eyed men with curved strong bows, never parted from killing, harry and rob travellers, to the far place he longs for.
34.nuance: The danger she names is his, not the woman's: the friend tries to hold him back by the robbers of the road rather than by the grief at home.

thinai_evidence.note: leaving her to cross the wastes

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the friend tries to stop the man's departure

35.reading: The woman says that the wasteland the man bent on wealth has gone into is, people say, a hot forest where a ghoul, gorged on the cut fat of men felled by the killing weapons of the curved-bowed Eyinar, sleeps in the wide shade of a hero-stone.
35.nuance: Everything on that road is at rest, the dead under the stone and the sated ghoul in its shade, while she has only report (என்பர்) to go on and no rest at all.

thinai_evidence.note: the Eyinar of the waste and the hot forest

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the waiting woman's fear for the man on the road

iraicchi.act: the elephant and his mate, deceived by the mirage, run to it together and fall together
iraicchi.sense: even beasts fooled by the waste do not part from their mates, yet the man leaves her

36.reading: The friend asks the good woman whether he will go to the hot forest of cracking heat, where an elephant takes the swift white mirage for water, runs to it together with his mate and falls with tangled legs, leaving her so that her bangles slip and fall.
36.nuance: The mirage deceives the pair but does not part them: they run and fall together, which is the reproach the friend leaves unspoken against the man who goes alone.

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the friend speaks of the man's going

37.reading: The mother asks whether the girl, who would falter as if about to fall when she played by the ford in front of the house with her friends around her, can now keep pace without lagging behind her lover on the stony paths of the wasteland.

thinai_evidence.note: going behind her lover through the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the mother after the daughter's elopement, to no named hearer

iraicchi.act: the stag, judging the pool's little water too scant for both, pretends to drink so that the doe may drink her fill
iraicchi.sense: the man whose heart has gone that way will see such care and his heart will turn back to the wife he left

38.reading: The friend tells the woman that the road the lover's heart has taken is, people say, a wasteland where a stag, judging that the little water in the pool will not be enough, wants the doe to drink her fill and only pretends to drink.
38.nuance: The stag's love is shown by a deceit (கள்ளத்தின் ஊச்சும்), and the poem sets it on the road the man's heart (உள்ளம்) has gone down, as if his heart had chosen the path where it would be taught tenderness. The words could also be the woman's own, said with the opposite edge.

thinai_evidence.note: the waste and its scant water

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the friend comforts the waiting woman (porul 5.35)

39.reading: The man tells his good heart that it is foolish: when they stir to set out after great wealth, she of bright ornaments cannot hold back, and sobs and sighs with swelling grief; how will she bear it once they have gone from her?
39.nuance: He argues from what he sees at the moment of setting out to what must follow after, so the sobbing he has watched becomes the measure of a grief he will not be there to see.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the man reasons with his heart against the journey

40.reading: The man tells his good heart that tonight it slept well in the cool place with the shoulders of her of the cool garland for companion; tomorrow, having crossed the wasteland of hill paths, alone, where will they lie down?
40.nuance: The cool (ஈர்ம், ஈர்ங்) of tonight is set against a tomorrow that has no place named at all; the question is the whole argument against going.

thinai_evidence.note: crossing the waste alone, away from her

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the poem; the colophon gives no thurai; the man on the eve of going speaks to his heart

links.note: Akananuru 99: the man leading the eloping girl bids her admire a forest strewn with murukku buds like the gripping claws of the striped tiger (கோள்உகிர் அன்ன). Aimpathu 31 uses the same simile, murukku buds like a tiger's blood-dyed claws, for the spring that breaks the waiting woman's heart.
links.teaches: Aimpathu 31 says outright that this season gives joy only to those who are together (எதிருநர்க்கு இன்பம்), and Akananuru 99 is that joy spoken by a man walking beside his girl, so the pair shows one flowering read as delight or as wound according to whether the lovers are together.

links.note: Kuruntokai 37: the friend tells the heroine that the road he took is a loving one, where the tusker strips the yaa branches to ease his mate's hunger. Aimpathu 32: on his road the tusker pours the little water of a rock pool over his heat-worn mate's head.
links.teaches: Kuruntokai 37 states the friend's conclusion itself, that the road is loving (அன்பின), while the Aimpathu gives only the tusker's act and leaves the inference to the heroine, so the pair shows the same comfort working first as a stated argument and then as an image she must read.

links.note: Akananuru 49: the foster mother remembers seeing that the girl who loved her parrot, ball and play-seeds (கிளியும், பந்தும், கழங்கும்) was not as before, without guessing why. Aimpathu 33: the girl no longer thinks of doll, ball, parrot and playmates, and the mother asks whether she will go after her lover.
links.teaches: In both the neglected playthings are the sign that the girl has passed out of childhood into love, but Akananuru 49 reads the sign too late and dwells on the mother's missed chance, while the venba reads it and turns at once to the burning road, so the pair shows the same evidence serving regret or foreboding.

links.note: Akananuru 369: after the daughter's elopement her parrot will not drink its milk, her playmates do not play and her doll gets no offering. Aimpathu 33: the girl herself has stopped thinking of doll, ball, parrot and playmates.
links.teaches: Aimpathu 33 says the girl has forgotten her toys and companions, and Akananuru 369 says those toys and companions still mourn her, so together they show the mother's grief as a forgetting that runs one way: the house keeps faith with a child who has already left it in mind.

links.note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving, tell me; if you mean to come back soon, tell it to those who will still be alive. Aimpathu 34: the friend asks the man whether he will cross many wastes of killing robbers, leaving the woman of sword-bright eyes.
links.teaches: Both are said to the man at the point of departure to stop him, but the Kural argues from the woman's death and the Aimpathu from the man's own danger among robbers, so the pair shows the two levers the dissuading speaker can pull against the journey, her life and his.

links.note: Akananuru 53: the woman says the man who loves wealth more than her crossed a waste where a red dog rests with its starving mate in the sweet shade of a lettered hero-stone (எழுத்துடை நடுகல் இன்நிழல்). Aimpathu 35: on the road of the man bent on wealth a ghoul gorged on the fat of the slain sleeps in a hero-stone's wide shade.
links.teaches: In both the hero-stone's shade is the only rest on the wealth-seeker's road, but Akananuru shelters a hungry pair there and the Aimpathu a sated ghoul alone, so the pair shows the stone's shade turned from a picture of shared hardship into one of the road's appetite for men, which is the woman's fear.

links.note: Akananuru 395: the woman says the man crossed a forest where a fork-horned stag, chasing the mirage, strays off the path and calls for its grazing doe in a failing voice. Aimpathu 36: an elephant pair takes the white mirage for water, runs to it together and falls with tangled legs.
links.teaches: The two poems take the same chase after a mirage to opposite ends: in Akananuru it parts the stag from its mate and gives the abandoned woman her own cry, in the Aimpathu the pair are fooled and fall together, so the image can either mirror her loneliness or shame the man who leaves when even deceived beasts do not part.

links.note: Naladiyar 398: the girl answers the friend who asks whether she can walk tomorrow behind her man through the hard forest: one who gets a great horse learns to ride it at once. Aimpathu 37: the mother asks whether the girl who faltered at play can keep pace behind her lover on the stony path. The mother doubts the feet that the girl says love will make able.
links.teaches: The same question, can her feet go with him, gets opposite answers: the mother measures the girl by her weakness at childhood play, the girl by the man she has gained, so across the two books the pair stages the quarrel of the elopement between the generation that remembers and the one that goes.

links.note: Akananuru 153: the foster mother says the girl who grew hot and tired even running after a ball with her friends has gone into the burning summer forest, and asks whether her tender feet can manage it (வல்லுநள் கொல்லோ). Aimpathu 37 asks the same with the same verb (வல்லவோ), recalling her faltering at play by the ford.
links.teaches: The verb வல் and the evidence from play recur in both, which shows the mother's doubt as a set argument of the form: she judges the girl's strength for the road only by her weakness at games, a measure that the girl's going has already overturned.

links.note: Kalittokai 11: the woman recalls that the man, calling the forest cruel, told her the tusker there lets his mate drink the little muddy water first and the stag gives its own shade to the doe. Aimpathu 38: the stag, judging the pool's little water too scant, feigns drinking so the doe drinks.
links.teaches: Kalittokai puts the beasts' care in the man's own report, so the woman reasons that one who saw and told it will not let her wither; Aimpathu 38 adds the stag's pretence, a deceit in the service of love, and sets it on the road his heart has already taken, so the same proof is offered from the friend's side and made finer.

links.note: Akananuru 371: a twist-horned stag whose mate was shot will not drink the little water of the pool (சில்நீர் உண்ணாது) and lies stricken; the man crossing alone sees it and thinks of his love's eyes. Aimpathu 38: the stag feigns drinking the pool's little water so the doe may drink.
links.teaches: Held together, the two stags at a pool of scant water show the paalai poets making the stag's not drinking the sign of love both while the mate lives and after she dies, and Akananuru 371 bears out the friend's hope in 38, since there the traveller does see such a stag and his thoughts turn home.

links.note: Akananuru 5: the man tells his heart he gave up the journey when his wife, without a word, showed her grief in her face and her sigh over their son. Aimpathu 39: the man calls his heart foolish, for when they stir to leave for wealth she sobs and sighs; how will she bear it once they are gone?
links.teaches: Akananuru 5 shows the journey given up on the sight of her mute grief, and Aimpathu 39 shows the man reasoning from her sobs at the setting out to the harder grief to come, so the pair gives the decision against wealth both as what he saw and as what he foresees.

links.note: Akananuru 167: the man asks his heart whether, after tonight with his wife in the tall mansion, they will lie tomorrow sleepless in the ruined hall of a deserted village. Aimpathu 40: after tonight on the shoulders of her of the cool garland, where will they lie tomorrow, alone beyond the hill paths?
links.teaches: Akananuru 167 answers its own question with a ruined lodging described in full, while Aimpathu 40 leaves the place unnamed (என்கொலே சேக்கும் இடம்), so the pair shows the same tonight-and-tomorrow argument against the journey working either by the horror of a described shelter or by the bare want of any.

source_issues: 31-40: the colophon gives only the thinai (பாலை) and no thurai; every thurai_akam speech situation is inferred from the poem, with occasion words null.
32 line 1: விலங்கல் is hard to construe here (a hill, or 'do not turn aside'), and செல்லாரோ வல்லர் can mean 'is he not able to go' or 'will he not come'; the verse is marked uncertain.
34 line 1: வல்லில் reads as a misprint for வல்வில் (strong bow).
36 line 3: வெடியோடும் is unclear (cracked ground, or bursts of heat); the reading takes it as the cracking heat of the forest.
39 line 2: மாற்றாள் is taken as 'cannot hold back (her grief)'; line 1 மாட்டோ டப் is split oddly and is read as மாட்டு ஓட, 'to run after'.
